title: Substantial Rights
description: Substantial rights decide whether a contractor can claim the R&D credit: the performer must keep a royalty-free right to use the research results.
summary: Substantial rights, under IRC § 41 and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d), determine whether a U.S. contractor performing research for a client can claim the federal R&D tax credit. A performer must retain a royalty-free right to use research results in its own business without client consent; otherwise, the research is treated as funded and excluded.

body.text: Substantial rights, under IRC § 41 and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d), determine whether a U.S. contractor performing research for a client can claim the federal R&D tax credit. A performer must retain a royalty-free right to use research results in its own business without client consent; otherwise, the research is treated as funded and excluded.
Executive Summary: Substantial Rights as the Gatekeeper of the Research Credit

Within the federal income tax framework governing the Credit for Increasing Research Activities under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 41, the doctrine of Substantial Rights (SR) functions as the primary legal determinant of which entity in a multi-party research arrangement constitutes the true economic investor entitled to claim Qualified Research Expenditures (QREs). Whenever a taxpayer performs research activities on behalf of another person or governmental entity, IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) mandates that the resulting expenditures be excluded from the performing taxpayer's eligible QRE base to the extent the research is "funded" by grant, contract, or otherwise. Under the governing Treasury Regulations, the funded research inquiry is structured as a conjunctive two-prong test—commonly termed the Dual Test—under which a performing contractor avoids the funded research exclusion only if it both retains Substantial Rights in the results of the research and bears the financial risk of the research because payment is contingent upon technical success.

Under this regulatory architecture, Substantial Rights operate as a strict threshold gatekeeper. To satisfy the Substantial Rights standard, the performing taxpayer must preserve an enduring, legally enforceable, and unrestricted proprietary right to utilize the resulting intellectual property (IP)—encompassing patents, formulas, software architectures, technical data, and underlying know-how—within its own trade or business without seeking subsequent client authorization and without paying royalties or licensing fees for that internal or commercial exploitation. From a tax policy perspective, this requirement ensures that the statutory subsidy under IRC § 41 rewards entities that do not merely execute contracted technical labor for hire, but rather internalize and retain reusable technological capital capable of driving subsequent domestic innovation and commercial competitiveness. When a performing entity surrenders the legal right to redeploy its technological discoveries across future commercial engagements, the federal tax system characterizes the performing entity as a commercial vendor compensated for services rather than an entrepreneurial innovator accumulating proprietary technical assets.

The operational significance of the Substantial Rights requirement is magnified by asymmetric regulatory outcomes that arise when contractual risk and intellectual property ownership are decoupled. If a performing contractor relinquishes all Substantial Rights by transferring exclusive ownership and usage rights to the client, the contractor is automatically barred from claiming the research credit under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(a)(3)(i) and § 1.41-4A(d)(2), regardless of how much financial risk the contractor assumed under the pricing structure of the agreement. Even more consequential is the regulatory compliance trap—referred to in practice as the "Disqualified Risk Trap" or the "neither party claims" rule—which occurs when a contractor performs research under a fixed-price or success-contingent contract (thereby bearing the financial risk) while the client retains exclusive ownership and all Substantial Rights to the research results. In that configuration, the performing contractor is disqualified for lacking Substantial Rights, while the paying client is simultaneously disqualified under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2) because its payment is contingent on the successful delivery of a finished result rather than an uncertain research process. Consequently, imprecise allocation of Substantial Rights in commercial and government contracts does not merely shift the tax benefit between contracting counterparties; it can permanently extinguish the IRC § 41 credit for the entire transaction.
Statutory and Regulatory Foundation of the Funded Research Exclusion
Qualified Research Expenses and the Computer Usage Distinction Under IRC Section 41

IRC § 41(a) and § 41(b) establish the statutory mechanics of the federal research credit, defining a taxpayer's QREs as the aggregate of in-house research expenses and contract research expenses paid or incurred during the taxable year in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer. Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A), in-house research expenses are strictly circumscribed to three expenditure categories: wages paid or incurred for qualified services performed by employees under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), amounts paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), and, under prescribed regulations, amounts paid or incurred to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii). By contrast, IRC § 41(b)(3) governs contract research expenses paid or incurred to an outside party to perform qualified research on the taxpayer's behalf.

A recurring source of interpretive confusion in audit practice involves distinguishing the general Substantial Rights standard under the funded research exclusion from a narrow statutory limitation applicable solely to the third category of in-house expenses—computer leasing costs. Specifically, IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(4) stipulate that amounts paid or incurred for the right to use computers in conducting qualified research do not qualify as in-house research expenses to the extent the taxpayer receives or accrues amounts from another person for the right to use "substantially identical personal property." While both doctrines employ overlapping terminology regarding "substantial" property or usage rights, their legal functions, statutory origins, and audit mechanics are entirely distinct. The "substantially identical personal property" rule under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) is a narrow anti-conduit netting provision restricted to computer leasing outlays, designed to prevent lessors or pass-through computer service conduits from claiming in-house research credits on leased hardware capacity that is simultaneously subleased or mirrored to third parties. Conversely, the Substantial Rights standard under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d) governs the macro-level determination of whether the substantive technological output of an entire research project is disqualified as funded research across all eligible expenditure categories.

body.text: The Regulatory Mechanics of IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4A(d)

To qualify for the credit, research activities must satisfy the four-part statutory definition of qualified research under IRC § 41(d)(1) while avoiding the statutory exclusions enumerated in IRC § 41(d)(4). Chief among these exclusions for commercial vendors, engineering firms, and defense contractors is IRC § 41(d)(4)(H), which excludes any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity. Because the statute itself does not define the term "funded," the substantive legal test is established by administrative regulations in Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(a)(3) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d).

Rigorous citation accuracy and conceptual separation between performer and payer rules are critical when applying these regulations. Under Title 26 of the Code of Federal Regulations, the substantive funded research rules are codified at 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d) (rather than an erroneous citation to "§ 1.41-4(d)"), whereas 26 CFR § 1.41-2(a)(3) serves as the threshold routing regulation for research performed for others. Furthermore, practitioners must avoid conflating the performing contractor's "funded research" exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d) with the paying customer's contract research rules under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e). Stating that a paying customer who lacks Substantial Rights fails the "funded research" exclusion misidentifies the governing regulatory provision. As a matter of strict regulatory law, the "funded research" exclusion applies to the entity performing the research, whereas a paying client that hires an outside vendor is governed by the contract research expense rules of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(1)–(3), which require that the agreement be entered into prior to performance, be performed "on behalf of" the taxpayer (requiring the paying client to hold Substantial Rights), and obligate the client to bear the expense even if the research is not successful.

For the performing taxpayer, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(a)(3) bifurcates contract performance into two mutually exclusive regulatory pathways based entirely on whether the performer retains Substantial Rights in the research results:

body.text: This regulatory bifurcation establishes a strict sequential hierarchy for audit examinations. Internal Revenue Service (IRS) examiners must evaluate IP retention (Substantial Rights) independently of, and prior to, financial exposure (Contingent Payment). If the performing contractor fails to retain Substantial Rights under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(a)(3)(i) and § 1.41-4A(d)(2), the expenditures are per se excluded from the performer's QREs, and no degree of financial loss or fixed-price risk assumed by the contractor can cure that defect.
Partially Funded Research and Mandatory Pro Rata Allocation

Unlike total disqualification under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(2) when Substantial Rights are absent, the retention of Substantial Rights unlocks partial credit preservation under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(3) when research is only partially funded. Specifically, if a taxpayer performing qualified research for another person retains Substantial Rights in the research results, the research is deemed funded only "to the extent of the payments (and fair market value of any property) to which the taxpayer becomes entitled by performing the research" on a non-contingent basis. Any excess qualified research expenditures incurred by the performing taxpayer above the guaranteed funding amount remain non-funded and eligible for the IRC § 41 credit.

When partial funding occurs, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(ii) imposes a mandatory pro rata allocation rule requiring the taxpayer to allocate the non-contingent funding across all qualified and non-qualified research expenses attributable to the project. Rather than allowing a performing contractor to allocate client reimbursements exclusively to non-qualified project costs first, the regulation requires that the funded portion be distributed proportionally across the project's expense base. Expressed mathematically, where Etotal represents total project research expenses (including qualified research expenses QREtotal and non-qualified research expenses Enon-qual), and Fguaranteed represents the non-contingent funding to which the performing taxpayer becomes entitled (with Fguaranteed < Etotal), the funded QREs (QREfunded) and the surviving eligible non-funded QREs (QREeligible) are determined as follows:
QREfunded = QREtotal × (Fguaranteed ÷ Etotal)
QREeligible = QREtotal − QREfunded = QREtotal × (1 − Fguaranteed ÷ Etotal)

Where all project research costs tracked for the engagement constitute otherwise qualified research expenses (Enon-qual = 0, so that Etotal = QREtotal), the pro rata formula simplifies directly to the excess of total QREs over guaranteed funding:
QREeligible = QREtotal − Fguaranteed

This mechanism is especially consequential in cost-sharing agreements, capped cost-reimbursement contracts, and voluntary cost-overrun scenarios where a contractor continues experimental development at its own expense after contractual funding limits have been exhausted. Because the contractor retained Substantial Rights under the underlying agreement, the self-funded overrun expenditures retain their character as eligible QREs. Conversely, if the exact extent of external funding cannot be determined at the time the taxpayer files its original federal income tax return for the taxable year, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(5) requires the taxpayer to treat the research as 100 percent funded on the initial return and subsequently file an amended return once the final funding amount is ascertained.
Definitional Analysis and Judicial Interpretation of Substantial Rights
The Standard of Unrestricted Proprietary Use

At its core, the Substantial Rights requirement measures whether the performing entity emerges from the research engagement with legally protected, commercially viable utility in the technological discoveries generated. To retain Substantial Rights under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(2), the performing taxpayer must preserve the right to use the results of the research in its trade or business without having to pay for that right—such as through running royalties, per-unit license fees, or buy-back charges—and without needing prior permission or discretionary consent from the contracting customer.

If a contract stipulates that the performing contractor may use the resulting technology only upon paying a royalty or licensing fee to the client, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(2) explicitly dictates that the performer retains no Substantial Rights. Similarly, contractual covenants that grant the customer absolute veto power over the contractor's subsequent use of developed know-how, or that restrict the contractor to using the technology solely to perform contracts for that specific customer, strip the retained right of independent commercial substance. Rather, the retained rights must allow the performing entity to internalize the resulting designs, algorithms, processes, or technical know-how and deploy them across future commercial offerings, internal manufacturing systems, or subsequent Independent Research and Development (IRAD) initiatives.
Why "Substantial" Does Not Mean "Exclusive": The Lockheed Martin Precedent

For decades following the enactment of the research credit, the IRS frequently asserted in examination and litigation that a contractor could not retain Substantial Rights if the customer obtained ownership of the contract deliverables or held the power to disclose or license the technical data to third-party competitors. That restrictive administrative posture was decisively rejected by the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit in the landmark decision Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000).

In Lockheed Martin, the taxpayer performed major defense research and development under fixed-price contracts with the U.S. government. Under the applicable Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) and defense acquisition clauses, the federal government obtained unlimited rights to use, duplicate, and disclose technical data and computer software generated under the contracts, including the right to provide that data to competing defense contractors for reprocurement. The government argued that because Lockheed Martin could not exclude others from using the research results and faced export and security restrictions on selling military technology to foreign buyers, its retained rights were "incidental" rather than "substantial."

The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of Federal Claims and rejected the government's equivalence between "substantial rights" and "exclusive rights," which the government had imported from patent capital gains tax law under IRC § 1235. Analyzing the explicit language of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(2) and (d)(3), the court held that the right to use the research results in the taxpayer's trade or business without paying for that right is, by itself, a Substantial Right, even when that right is non-exclusive and shared with the client. Specifically, because Lockheed Martin retained the unrestricted, royalty-free right to use the developed technical know-how, engineering processes, and non-patented technologies in manufacturing products for other customers and bidding on subsequent contracts, it satisfied the Substantial Rights test.

The Lockheed Martin precedent preserves the viability of the IRC § 41 credit across industries—most notably aerospace, defense, systems integration, and custom enterprise software—where shared IP licensing and retained "background/foreground know-how" clauses are standard commercial practice. Nevertheless, post-Lockheed Martin jurisprudence and administrative guidance emphasize that the retained right must still be legally and practically real: if a contract vests the client with "ultimate power" over the IP by requiring complete assignment of all inventions and know-how coupled with nondisclosure or non-use covenants that bar the contractor from using the learned technology in its own business without prior client consent, Substantial Rights are negated.
The Dual Test Interplay: Substantial Rights and Financial Risk
The Contingency Standard and Contract Pricing Archetypes

While Substantial Rights establish proprietary eligibility, the second prong of the Dual Test under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(1) requires that payment to the performing contractor be "contingent on the success of the research." Regulations treat non-contingent payments as funding the uncertain research activity itself, whereas payments contingent upon successful technical performance are treated as amounts paid to purchase the resulting product or deliverable once technical uncertainty has been resolved at the contractor's risk.

In practice, IRS examiners and tax practitioners evaluate contract pricing models as initial structural proxies for the financial risk prong, while pairing them with IP ownership clauses to evaluate Substantial Rights. Fixed-price contracts generally satisfy the financial risk requirement for the performing contractor because the contractor must deliver a technically functioning product or milestone for a predetermined price; if the research fails or incurs cost overruns, the contractor absorbs the financial loss without reimbursement. Conversely, cost-plus, cost-reimbursable, time-and-materials (T&M), and hourly rate contracts generally fail the financial risk standard for the performing contractor because the customer guarantees reimbursement for hours worked and materials consumed regardless of whether the technical objectives succeed or fail.
The Four-Scenario Dual Test Eligibility Framework

The interaction between the Substantial Rights standard and the Financial Risk (Contingent Payment) standard produces four distinct regulatory outcomes governing which party—the performing contractor, the paying client, or neither—is legally entitled to claim the IRC § 41 credit:

body.text: Second-Order Analysis of Scenario 3: The "Neither Party Claims" Compliance Trap

Scenario 3 represents one of the most severe structural traps in federal R&D tax law. In conventional commercial procurement, corporate buyers routinely negotiate contracts that combine two buyer-favorable provisions: a fixed-price payment schedule contingent upon formal acceptance of a working prototype or software platform, and a comprehensive "work made for hire" or exclusive IP assignment clause vesting 100 percent of all resulting patents, source code, technical data, and know-how solely in the buyer.

While commercially advantageous to the buyer from a procurement perspective, this contractual pairing bifurcates the two essential attributes of an eligible R&D claimant across separate legal entities. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(a)(3)(i) and § 1.41-4A(d)(2), the performing vendor's surrender of Substantial Rights automatically classifies the research as "funded" from the vendor's perspective, eliminating the vendor's ability to claim in-house QREs even though the vendor bore 100 percent of the financial risk of technical failure. Simultaneously, when the paying client attempts to claim 65 percent of the contract payments as contract research expenses under IRC § 41(b)(3) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2), the IRS disallows the client's claim because the client's obligation to pay was contingent upon the successful delivery of the finished work product. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2), amounts paid under a success-contingent arrangement are characterized as capital or operational expenditures for the purchase of a completed asset rather than expenditures for the conduct of uncertain research.

The second-order economic implication of Scenario 3 is that the IRC § 41 tax expenditure is intentionally designed to require unity of entrepreneurial risk and retained technological utility within a single taxpayer. Where a contractor bears financial exposure without retaining Substantial Rights, tax law characterizes the contractor not as an innovator investing in reusable technological capital, but as a commercial vendor furnishing a performance warranty on a contracted deliverable. Moreover, even when parties avoid Scenario 3 by shifting to a non-contingent reimbursement structure (Scenario 2 or Scenario 4) so that the paying client can claim the research credit under IRC § 41(b)(3), the statutory 65 percent limitation on contract research expenses reduces the aggregate QRE base by 35 percent compared to Scenario 1, where the performing contractor claims 100 percent of its eligible in-house wage and supply expenditures.
Applied Contractual Analysis and Worked Examples
Defense and Government Contracting Model (Hypothetical Worked Example 1)

To illustrate the operational mechanics of the Dual Test under Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d), consider a hypothetical scenario grounded in the governing regulatory framework. Suppose Contractor Alpha, a domestic defense technology engineering corporation, executes a firm fixed-price contract with a U.S. federal agency for $4,000,000 to design and develop a novel encrypted satellite communication software protocol. Under the contract terms, payment of the $4,000,000 price is strictly contingent upon the protocol passing rigorous technical acceptance testing, and any research cost overruns must be absorbed entirely by Contractor Alpha. During the taxable year, Contractor Alpha incurs $3,200,000 in qualified employee wages and $300,000 in qualified research supplies, totaling $3,500,000 in otherwise eligible in-house QREs.

The contract's Intellectual Property and Data Rights clauses provide that the U.S. government receives legal title to the final deliverable software code and a perpetual, non-exclusive, irrevocable, royalty-free license to use, modify, reproduce, and disclose all underlying technical data generated during the contract. However, the contract explicitly states that Contractor Alpha retains an unrestricted, perpetual, royalty-free right to utilize all underlying technical specifications, mathematical algorithms, system architectures, and engineering processes developed during the engagement in its own business operations—including integrating those algorithms into commercial enterprise products and bidding on future government or private-sector contracts—without seeking agency approval or paying royalties.

Applying the Dual Test to Contractor Alpha begins with the threshold evaluation of Substantial Rights under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(a)(3)(ii) and § 1.41-4A(d)(2). Although the federal agency holds title to the deliverable software and retains non-exclusive unlimited data rights, Contractor Alpha is not required to hold exclusive rights under the Federal Circuit's holding in Lockheed Martin. Because Contractor Alpha retains a legally enforceable, unrestricted, royalty-free right to exploit the underlying algorithms and technical know-how in its own trade or business without prior client approval, this retained proprietary usage right—often termed a "shop right" or retained data right—satisfies the Substantial Rights standard. Turning to the second prong under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(1), the firm fixed-price structure ensures that payment is contingent upon passing technical acceptance testing and that Contractor Alpha bears full financial exposure for cost overruns or technical failure, thereby satisfying the financial risk standard. Because both prongs of the Dual Test are satisfied under Scenario 1, none of the research is treated as funded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H). Recomputing Contractor Alpha's eligible QREs step by step yields the following result:
QREtotal = Wagesqual + Suppliesqual = $3,200,000 + $300,000 = $3,500,000
Non-Contingent Funding (Fguaranteed) = $0 (100% Contingent on Technical Acceptance under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1))
QREfunded = $0
QREeligible = QREtotal − QREfunded = $3,500,000 − $0 = $3,500,000

Partially Funded Research and Pro Rata Allocation (Hypothetical Worked Example 2)

To illustrate the quantitative impact of retaining versus relinquishing Substantial Rights in a partially funded cost-overrun arrangement under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(2) and § 1.41-4A(d)(3), consider a second hypothetical scenario. Assume Engineering Firm Beta enters into a research and development agreement with Client Gamma to develop an advanced composite structural material. Under the agreement, Client Gamma agrees to reimburse Engineering Firm Beta on a non-contingent time-and-materials basis up to a maximum funding cap of $600,000, payable regardless of whether the composite material achieves the target tensile strength. Engineering Firm Beta encounters unexpected technical uncertainties and voluntarily continues the research at its own expense after exhausting the $600,000 cap, incurring a total of $1,000,000 in otherwise eligible in-house QREs (with $0 of non-qualified research costs on the project) during the taxable year.

The tax consequences of this $400,000 self-funded cost overrun diverge dramatically depending on the IP terms of the contract. In Variant A (Substantial Rights Retained), the contract grants Client Gamma ownership of the physical test batches, while Engineering Firm Beta explicitly retains a perpetual, royalty-free right to use the developed chemical formulations and curing processes in its own business for future commercial clients. Conversely, in Variant B (No Substantial Rights Retained), the contract assigns 100 percent of all inventions, formulations, processes, and know-how exclusively to Client Gamma and prohibits Engineering Firm Beta from using the technology for any other customer without paying a licensing fee.

Under Variant A, because Engineering Firm Beta retains Substantial Rights, the research is not automatically disqualified under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(2). Instead, under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i), the research is treated as funded only to the extent of the non-contingent payments to which Beta becomes entitled ($600,000). Applying the pro rata allocation rule of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(ii) across the $1,000,000 of total project QREs preserves the excess self-funded expenditure:
Funded Ratio (Variant A) = Fguaranteed ÷ Etotal = $600,000 ÷ $1,000,000 = 60%
QREfunded (Variant A) = QREtotal × (Fguaranteed ÷ Etotal) = $1,000,000 × 60% = $600,000
QREeligible (Variant A) = QREtotal − QREfunded = $1,000,000 − $600,000 = $400,000

Thus, under Variant A, Engineering Firm Beta is entitled to claim $400,000 of QREs attributable to its self-funded overrun, while Client Gamma may evaluate the $600,000 non-contingent payment under the contract research rules of IRC § 41(b)(3) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e). In stark contrast, under Variant B, because Engineering Firm Beta retains no Substantial Rights in the research results, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(a)(3)(i) and § 1.41-4A(d)(2) mandate that the entire research project be treated as fully funded, regardless of the fact that Beta bore 100 percent of the financial loss on the $400,000 overrun:
QREfunded (Variant B) = 100% × QREtotal = $1,000,000 (Per Se Disqualification under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2))
QREeligible (Variant B) = QREtotal − QREfunded = $1,000,000 − $1,000,000 = $0

body.text: Tax Compliance, Audit Substantiation, and Statutory Intersections
IRS Audit Techniques Guide Standards and Contractual Substantiation

Because the funded research inquiry is governed by the express terms of the agreement entered into between the performing taxpayer and its customer, IRS examinations of IRC § 41 claims focus heavily on documentary contract review. The IRS Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) for the Credit for Increasing Research Activities instructs examining agents to request and inspect the complete contractual record—including Master Services Agreements (MSAs), individual Statements of Work (SOWs), task orders, purchase orders, contract modifications, and incorporated regulatory clauses—to evaluate both the payment contingency terms and the allocation of IP rights.

To withstand examination scrutiny—which has intensified following heightened IRS disclosure requirements and judicial decisions addressing claim specificity such as Harper—taxpayers cannot rely on oral understandings or post-hoc characterizations of how research outputs were used. First, the written contract itself must affirmatively preserve the performing taxpayer's proprietary right to use the research results in its trade or business without restriction or royalty obligation. Second, as a matter of evidentiary corroboration, performing taxpayers should maintain contemporaneous internal records demonstrating the actual operational exercise of those retained Substantial Rights—such as engineering logs showing how technical data or algorithms developed under a customer contract were subsequently integrated into the taxpayer's internal IRAD pipeline or deployed in commercial product lines sold to third parties.

body.text: Interaction with IRC Section 174 and Section 174A Capitalization and Expensing Rules

Beyond the four corners of IRC § 41, a taxpayer's eligibility to claim QREs is statutorily linked to IRC § 174: under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A), qualified research expenses must first qualify as research or experimental (R&E) expenditures treatable under IRC § 174. Recent federal tax legislation—specifically the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA)—reinstated immediate domestic expensing for domestic R&E expenditures under IRC § 174A.

Despite the restoration of immediate domestic R&E deductibility under IRC § 174A, the funded research exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and the Substantial Rights standard remain rigid prerequisites for claiming the IRC § 41 tax credit. Even if a contractor's costs constitute deductible business or R&E outlays, any failure to retain Substantial Rights disqualifies those expenditures from the IRC § 41 QRE base. Furthermore, statutory coordination rules codified under IRC § 280C(c) require taxpayers claiming the full IRC § 41 research credit to reduce their corresponding IRC § 174A deduction (or decrease their capitalized IRC § 174 amortization base) by the amount of the research credit claimed, unless the taxpayer timely elects a reduced credit rate. This statutory linkage reinforces the foundational principle that eligible research expenditures must be incurred for the direct benefit of the claiming taxpayer's own trade or business—a nexus established by the retention of Substantial Rights.
Recommendations for Clarifying and Securing Substantial Rights

Given the high audit friction surrounding modern IP sharing agreements, cloud software licensing, and hybrid government procurement vehicles, both policymakers and corporate tax practitioners require structured mechanisms to reduce ambiguity in applying the Substantial Rights standard.
Modernization of Treasury Regulations and Administrative Safe Harbors

Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d) was drafted in an era dominated by traditional manufacturing and brick-and-mortar engineering contracts and has not been comprehensively updated to reflect contemporary multi-tenant software development, open-source integration, data-rights splitting, or modern federal acquisition models. The Department of the Treasury and the IRS should promulgate updated regulatory guidance that formally codifies the Federal Circuit's holding in Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, explicitly stating in the regulatory text that a non-exclusive, perpetual, royalty-free right to use research results in the taxpayer's trade or business satisfies the Substantial Rights requirement without any requirement to exclude third parties. Additionally, administrative safe harbors should be established to define bright-line parameters for acceptable retained background/foreground know-how licenses and to clearly distinguish the funded research Substantial Rights test (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)) from the computer leasing exclusion for "substantially identical personal property" (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(4)).
Proactive Utilization of Private Letter Rulings (PLRs)

When taxpayers enter into complex joint development agreements, cost-sharing consortia, or novel licensing structures where the retention of Substantial Rights is legally ambiguous, practitioners should evaluate requesting a Private Letter Ruling (PLR) from the IRS Office of Chief Counsel prior to filing the tax return. A PLR provides a binding written determination applying the tax laws to the taxpayer's specific factual and contractual arrangement, offering audit certainty regarding whether the agreement preserves Substantial Rights. Although a PLR may not be cited or used as binding legal precedent by other taxpayers, a body of consistent PLR determinations frequently informs subsequent published IRS revenue rulings and administrative guidance.
Contractual Drafting Standards and Pre-Execution Tax Review

Because post-execution audit defense cannot rewrite an unfavorable IP clause, corporate tax departments must integrate into the commercial contracting workflow before MSAs and SOWs are executed. Where a performing contractor seeks to preserve IRC § 41 credit eligibility on fixed-price engagements, the agreement should incorporate an explicit reservation-of-rights clause stating that, notwithstanding any transfer of title in physical or software deliverables to the client, the contractor retains a non-exclusive, irrevocable, perpetual, paid-up, royalty-free, worldwide license to use all underlying technical data, inventions, algorithms, processes, and know-how developed during the engagement in its own trade or business—expressly including internal R&D, testing, and commercial sales to third parties—without requiring subsequent client approval or royalty payments. Conversely, where a paying customer intends to claim contract research expenses under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e), the customer must ensure both that it bears the financial risk of unsuccessful research (avoiding Scenario 3 fixed-price contingencies) and that vendor agreements do not strip the customer of Substantial Rights through restrictive "black box" licensing fees.
Continuous Judicial and Legislative Monitoring

Finally, tax professionals must continuously monitor post-Lockheed Martin federal court litigation and IRS Chief Counsel advisories addressing funded research, contract sampling methodologies, and project-level substantiation. Concurrently, ongoing tracking of legislative and administrative guidance implementing IRC § 41, IRC § 174, and IRC § 174A under the OBBBA is essential to ensure that contract structuring, pro rata partial-funding allocations, and credit-deduction coordination elections remain fully aligned with evolving federal tax law.
